name: Boston
headline: Brownstones on filled marsh, three-deckers on the hills,
and every commuter rail line running home to it.
answer: Boston is the capital of Massachusetts, a Suffolk County city of 675,647 people (2020 Census) made up of 23 neighborhoods. Its housing is mostly attached and multi-unit: brownstone and brick row houses near the center, and triple-deckers, mostly built between the 1880s and 1930s, farther out. Single-family sales are a small and unrepresentative slice of the market: The Warren Group's Boston row counted 50 in 2025 against 1,611 condo sales, and it reports neighborhoods such as Dorchester, Jamaica Plain and Charlestown on separate rows. Every MBTA commuter rail line ends at South Station or North Station, and I-93 and I-90 meet downtown.
overview: Puritan settlers founded Boston on the Shawmut Peninsula in 1630, set aside Boston Common in 1634 and opened Boston Latin School in 1635. Much of today's city is made land: the South End was built on tidal marsh beginning in 1849, and the Back Bay was filled between 1857 and about 1882, which is why their streets run in regular grids of Victorian row houses. Boston became a city in 1822 and grew by annexation, taking in Roxbury in 1868, Dorchester in 1870, Charlestown, Brighton (including present-day Allston) and West Roxbury, which included Jamaica Plain, in 1874, and Hyde Park in 1912.

The city recognizes 23 neighborhoods, from Beacon Hill and the North End to Hyde Park and West Roxbury. On Beacon Hill, Federal-style brick row houses, the first built between 1803 and 1805, climb toward Charles Bulfinch's gold-domed State House of 1798. Frederick Law Olmsted's Emerald Necklace links about 1,100 acres of parks over 7 miles, from the Back Bay Fens through Jamaica Pond and the Arnold Arboretum to Franklin Park. The Big Dig, which concluded in December 2007, moved the elevated Central Artery of I-93 into tunnels, and the Rose Kennedy Greenway opened on the vacated land in October 2008. The 2.5-mile Freedom Trail runs from downtown to the Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown, and public ferries reach several of the Boston Harbor Islands. This is one city guide for now; neighborhood guides are planned.

Boston plans its own zoning: the state's MBTA Communities rules do not apply, because Boston is exempt from the Zoning Act, including Section 3A. A city ordinance signed in April 2024 created the Boston Planning Department, and most former Boston Planning and Development Agency staff moved into it that July. The Zoning Commission adopted six Squares + Streets districts on April 17, 2024, allowing mixed-use buildings and multifamily housing in neighborhood centers near transit; Mattapan Square was mapped first, in May 2024, Roslindale Square followed on May 22, 2025, and a December 2025 amendment added two more district types. Since October 2024, projects of seven or more units must make 20 percent of them income-restricted, up from 13 percent. In 2024 the city approved projects totaling 3,575 net new residential units, 1,210 of them income-restricted.

housing.text: Boston's triple-deckers were mostly built between the 1880s and 1930s, and the city has studied new versions of the type for neighborhoods including Roxbury, Mattapan, Dorchester and Hyde Park. Near the center, the Back Bay, South End and Charlestown are known for 19th-century brownstone and brick row houses. Condominiums dominate sales: The Warren Group counted 1,611 condo sales and 50 single-family sales on its 2025 Boston row, so the single-family median of about $3.1 million describes a very small set of homes and not the city as a whole.

villages.name: Beacon Hill
villages.line: About a sixth of a square mile between Boston Common and the Charles River Esplanade, with Federal-style brick row houses, brick sidewalks, gas lamps and the Greek Revival townhouses of Louisburg Square; a National Historic Landmark since 1962.

villages.name: Back Bay
villages.line: Former tidal flats filled between 1857 and about 1882, laid out with Victorian brownstone row houses along Commonwealth Avenue's center mall, with Copley Square at its southeast corner.

villages.name: South End
villages.line: Built on tidal marsh beside Boston Neck from 1849, with brick and brownstone row houses from 1850 to 1880 around small residential squares; often described as the largest intact Victorian row-house district in the country.

villages.name: Jamaica Plain
villages.line: Part of Roxbury, then West Roxbury, until annexed to Boston in 1874, with triple-deckers from the 1870s onward, Jamaica Pond, and four Orange Line stations under the Southwest Corridor Park.

villages.name: Charlestown
villages.line: Laid out by Thomas Graves and settled in 1629, annexed to Boston in 1874, with red-brick row houses, the Bunker Hill Monument and the Charlestown Navy Yard.

villages.name: Dorchester
villages.line: A separate town founded in 1630 and part of Boston since 1870; the city's largest neighborhood at more than 6 square miles, with many three-decker buildings and stations on the Red Line and the Fairmount Line.

rail.line: South Station (Red Line, Silver Line SL1-SL3; Fairmount, Fall River/New Bedford, Framingham/Worcester, Franklin/Foxboro, Greenbush, Kingston, Needham and Providence/Stoughton Lines)
North Station (Orange and Green Lines; Fitchburg, Haverhill, Lowell and Newburyport/Rockport Lines; Amtrak Downeaster)
Back Bay (Orange Line, commuter rail and Amtrak)

commute.text: Boston is the hub of the MBTA: the Red, Orange, Blue and Green Lines and the Mattapan Line run through the city, and commuter rail ends at South Station or North Station, with Back Bay as a through stop. Amtrak's Acela and Northeast Regional leave from South Station and Back Bay, and the Downeaster from North Station. I-93 and I-90 meet downtown in the tunnels built by the Big Dig, US 1 crosses the Tobin Bridge, and MBTA ferries link the waterfront with Charlestown, Hingham, Hull and other harbor communities.

places.name: Boston Common
places.line: Founded in 1634, with ballfields, a tot lot and the Frog Pond, which is open for skating in winter and has a spray area in summer.

places.name: Freedom Trail
places.line: A 2.5-mile path through downtown and Charlestown linking sites of Boston National Historical Park, including Faneuil Hall and the Old South Meeting House.

places.name: Charlestown Navy Yard
places.line: One of the country's first naval shipyards, home to USS Constitution and the museum ship USS Cassin Young.

places.name: Emerald Necklace
places.line: Frederick Law Olmsted's 1,100-acre chain of eight parks over 7 miles, from Charlesgate and the Back Bay Fens to Franklin Park.

places.name: Arnold Arboretum
places.line: A 281-acre preserve founded in 1872 and part of the Emerald Necklace, free and open every day.

places.name: Boston Harbor Islands
places.line: A national and state park of 34 islands and peninsulas, with public ferries to Spectacle, Georges and Peddocks Islands among others.

places.name: Rose Kennedy Greenway
places.line: A 1.5-mile park opened in October 2008 on the land freed when the Big Dig removed the elevated highway, with the Greenway Carousel.

history.text: Puritan settlers founded Boston on the Shawmut Peninsula, naming the town on September 7, 1630 (Old Style).
Boston Common was set aside, now described as the nation's first public park.
Boston was incorporated as a city on March 19, 1822.
The Tremont Street subway opened, the first subway in the United States.
The Big Dig concluded in December, having rerouted the elevated Central Artery of I-93 into the O'Neill Tunnel; the Rose Kennedy Greenway was created in the space the elevated roadway left.

tax.note: Split rate: commercial, industrial and personal property pay $26.96 per $1,000 in FY2026 (DLS Tax Rates by Class). Residential exemption: the City Council set it at 35% of the average assessed value of Class One residential parcels for FY2026 (FY26 Tax Classification order, https://www.boston.gov/sites/default/files/file/2025/12/FY26%20Tax%20Classification%20order.pdf). The maximum exempt amount, $351,108 (up to $4,353.74 in tax), is from a January 22, 2026 Jamaica Plain Gazette op-ed (https://jamaicaplaingazette.com/2026/01/22/op-ed-your-property-matters-fy-2026-boston-residential-tax-exemption-can-save-you-up-to-4353-74-on-your-property-tax-bill/), not a city document; verify with the Assessing Department. Fact-check 2026-10-22: confirmed on the City of Boston Assessing page 'How we tax your property' (2026 tax rate: residential $12.40; commercial, industrial, personal property $26.96) and the FY26 Tax Classification order (35% residential exemption, minimum residential factor), https://www.boston.gov/departments/assessing/how-we-tax-your-property.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Boston, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price on its Boston row for calendar year 2025 was $3,092,500, across 50 sales. In 2024 it was $3,100,000, across 51 sales. That is not a citywide median, and it is a small and unrepresentative sample: the same row counted 1,611 condo sales in 2025 at a median of $945,000, and neighborhoods such as Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Charlestown and West Roxbury are reported on separate rows.

faq.q: Why is the single-family median on Boston's Warren Group row so high?
faq.a: Boston is mostly condominiums, triple-deckers and other multi-unit buildings, so few single-family homes trade on The Warren Group's Boston row: 50 in 2025. A handful of high-priced sales can set the median. Condo sales on the same row numbered 1,611, at a median of $945,000.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Boston, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Boston's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $12.40 per $1,000 of assessed value, and commercial, industrial and personal property pay $26.96. Boston's residential exemption for owner-occupants is 35% of the average residential assessed value in FY2026, under the City Council's classification order; the Assessing Department confirms the dollar amount.

faq.q: How is Boston changing its zoning for new housing?
faq.a: Boston is exempt from the state Zoning Act, including the MBTA Communities law, and sets its own rules. Squares + Streets districts, adopted on April 17, 2024, allow mixed-use and multifamily buildings in neighborhood centers near transit and were mapped first in Mattapan Square and then in Roslindale Square. Since October 2024, projects of seven or more units must make 20 percent of them income-restricted.
